parts: Infancy (birth to 2 years), early childhood (2 to 6 years, the preschool stage), middle childhood (6 to 11 years) and adolescence (12 to 19 years). Infancy is the foundation of all development.

The sequence is fairly uniform across cultures but individual differences are large (one child walks at 10 months, another at 24). Milestones: lifting chin 1 month, rolling over 4 months, sitting alone 8 months, crawling 9 months, standing independently 9–10 months, walking alone about 15 months, running and climbing stairs 2 years, riding a tricycle 3 years, throwing a ball overhead 4 years, copying complex figures 6 years. Motor development supports the mother–child bond and mastery over the body. Gross motor development is control over large muscle groups (crawling, standing, walking). Fine motor development is control over small muscles of hands and fingers (grasping, pinching, holding a pencil).

Early childhood: locomotion becomes graceful; a 3-year-old runs straight and jumps; a 4-year-old skips, hops on one foot and catches a large ball; 5–6-year-olds ride a bicycle with training wheels and use the slide and swing. Fine motor: 2–3 years copies a circle and buttons large buttons; 3–5 years copies a square, prints own name and ties shoelaces; 5–7 years copies a triangle and prints numerals. Hand preference begins at 3–4 years; most children are toilet-trained by 4. Middle childhood: growth is gradual until the puberty growth spurt at 11–13; girls are slightly shorter than boys at 6–8 years but then taller and heavier; the spurt comes earlier in girls; children gain strength, speed, coordination and enjoy outdoor games.

Piaget's stages: sensori-motor (birth–2), pre-operational (2–7), concrete operational (7–11) and formal operational (11+). Early childhood is the pre-operational stage with two sub-stages: symbolic function (2–4 years: mental images and symbols, pretend play, drawing; egocentrism – inability to see from another's point of view) and intuitive thought (4–7 years: asks 'why' and 'how come'; centration – focusing on one characteristic). Attention span grows (a 3-year-old 15–20 minutes, a 6-year-old an hour). Language explosion: about 900 words at 3 years and 8,000–14,000 by 6; grammar rules appear; bilingual children understand language better. Middle childhood (concrete operational): logical principles (conservation, transformation, seriation), better spatial reasoning, logical thinking limited to real and concrete situations, abstract concepts remain hard; language: synonyms, antonyms, prefixes and suffixes.

Early childhood: self-conscious emotions (shame, guilt), ability to modify emotional expression to the situation, empathy (depends on cognitive and language development), learning to control anger through guidance and role models. Play: parallel play (beside, not with), cooperative play (small group, pretend play), rough-and-tumble play (running, racing; learning to take turns and rules). Middle childhood: social comparison, seeing others' perspectives, pride and shame, mixed emotions, concealing emotions, internalised values and moral judgment; girls value interpersonal relations and family, boys social prestige; bullying (bullies often have demanding but unresponsive parents; victims are depressed with low self-esteem); self-concept shifts to personality traits and moves towards identity. Peer acceptance is important for self-esteem; a child liked by some and disliked by others is 'controversial'; temperament is an internal determiner of emotional development.

Socialization is the process of acquiring norms, values and beliefs significant in society and transmitting cultural values to children, including regulating and disciplining behaviour. Agents: parents and family, peers, school, religious institutions and mass media. In early childhood the family is primary; in middle childhood peers and school become prominent and stereotypes and prejudices develop. Parenting styles: authoritarian (demanding, controlling, insensitive), permissive (indulgent, non-demanding), authoritative (firm, consistent, gives reasons for discipline) and neglectful/uninvolved (uncaring, low control and communication). Ethnicity and socio-economic status also influence child development.
